Professional development to increase teacher behavior‐specific praise: A single‐case design replication
Nicholas A. Gage, Nicolette M. Grasley‐Boy, Ashley S. MacSuga‐Gage
Abstract Effective classroom instruction is contingent upon successful classroom management. Unfortunately, not all teachers successfully manage classroom behavior and need in‐service professional development. In this study, we replicated a targeted professional development approach that included a brief one‐on‐one training session and emailed visual performance feedback to increase novice teachers’ use of behavior‐specific praise, an evidence‐based classroom management skill. Dependent variables collected through direct observation included teachers’ behavior‐specific praise along with average student engagement and disruptions. Four elementary teachers participated and, based on a multiple‐baseline single‐case design, we found a functional relationship between the targeted professional development and teachers’ increased use of behavior‐specific praise. decisions.reason: The current source (Gage, Grasley-Boy, & MacSuga-Gage, 2018, 10.1002/pits.22106) remains restricted to its title, abstract, and 56 publisher-deposited references with no body upgrade. The abstract states that the authors replicated a targeted professional development (PD) approach including a brief one-on-one training session and emailed visual performance feedback to increase novice teachers' use of behavior-specific praise (BSP), measuring teacher BSP, student engagement, and disruptions across four elementary teachers in a multiple-baseline design, without naming the replicated study in the abstract. Deposited references include both shipped row 209 (e_1_2_11_24_1: Gage, MacSuga-Gage, & Crews, 2017, 10.1177/1098300717693568) and Rathel, Drasgow, Brown, & Marshall (2014 print / 2013 online, e_1_2_11_42_1, 10.1177/1098300713492856), alongside other feedback studies (e.g., Barton, 2013; Artman-Meeker, 2012; Sanetti, 2013). Newly verified original abstracts show that Gage et al. (2017) tested a two-tier PD model (a 25-min didactic training in Study 1 plus emailed visual performance feedback in Study 2) on elementary teachers' BSP, whereas Rathel et al. (2014) tested emailed performance feedback with progress-monitoring graphs on induction-level teachers' BSP and student task engagement. Without the current full text, whether the replicated approach binds to row 209, Rathel et al. (2014), or a chain of both is undeterminable.

The current source (a9fa5691229969ab.txt) consists only of the title, abstract, and 56 deposited references. The abstract states that the authors replicated a targeted professional development (PD) approach combining a brief one-on-one training session and emailed visual performance feedback to increase novice elementary teachers' behavior-specific praise (BSP), measuring teacher BSP, student engagement, and disruptions across four elementary teachers in a multiple-baseline design. However, the deposited references contain competing overlapping candidates that cannot be disambiguated without the current full text: shipped row 209 (e_1_2_11_24_1, Gage, MacSuga-Gage, & Crews, 2017, 10.1177/1098300717693568), whose verified primary abstract (03_gage_metadata.body) evaluates a targeted PD package combining a brief initial training session with emailed visual performance feedback on elementary teachers' BSP in a multiple-baseline design; and Rathel, Drasgow, Brown, & Marshall (e_1_2_11_42_1, 2014 print / 2013 online, 10.1177/1098300713492856), whose verified primary abstract (5142d77b.../attempt_1.body) evaluates emailed graphic performance feedback on four induction-level novice teachers' BSP and student task engagement (without describing a brief one-on-one training session in its abstract), alongside other feedback studies (e.g., e_1_2_11_7_1 Barton et al., 2013). Because the abstract never cites which study or studies define the replicated target or whether both Gage et al. (2017) and Rathel et al. (2014) are retested, missing_row remains undeterminable.
